summary: A hard-fighting anadromous herring relative that runs up Maritime rivers by the tens of thousands each spring — the Saint John River near Mactaquac in New Brunswick and several Nova Scotia rivers, especially the Annapolis, are the region's best-known runs. Often called "the poor man's salmon" for the sport it offers on light tackle.

sections.heading: Know the Fish
sections.body_md:
American shad (*Alosa sapidissima*) are the largest member of the herring family in Atlantic Canada — deep-bodied, strongly compressed, silvery fish with a row of dark spots trailing back from the shoulder. They're anadromous: adults live at sea and run up freshwater rivers each spring to spawn, arriving in the Saint John Region in numbers described as being visible "by the tens of thousands" during the peak of the run. Typical rod-caught fish run 1-3.5 kg (2-8 lb), and despite their herring-family lineage, they pull hard and jump, which is exactly why anglers call them the poor man's salmon.

Shad do not feed during their spawning migration, so strikes are believed to be triggered by aggression, reflex, or simple annoyance at a lure invading their space rather than genuine feeding behavior — which affects how you need to fish for them.

sections.heading: Where to Find Them
sections.body_md:
**New Brunswick:** the Saint John River is the region's headline shad water, with the spring run concentrating around **Mactaquac** — the Mactaquac Dam (built 1967) has historically been a bottleneck/counting point for the run, though DFO has moved to close the Mactaquac Biodiversity Facility that supported the population, a development worth watching for anyone planning trips around this fishery in future years.

**Nova Scotia:** the **Annapolis River** is internationally known as one of the best places anywhere to catch American shad, with fish entering by the thousands in season and fifty-fish days reported as realistic on a good day, in the right spot. The **Shubenacadie River, Stewiacke River, and Nine Mile River**, along with several rivers through the Annapolis Valley, all carry healthy shad runs as well. On the Stewiacke specifically, look for fast-moving water no more than a couple of feet deep to find catchable fish.

sections.heading: When to Go
sections.body_md: Spring is the entire game with this species — shad push into Maritime rivers to spawn as water temperatures rise, with the Saint John Region run typically visible through spring, and Nova Scotia's Annapolis Valley rivers seeing their runs on a similar spring timetable. Within a day, dawn and dusk (the sudden light change) are frequently when the bite turns on hardest, sometimes triggering large numbers of fish to strike within a short window.

sections.heading: Gear
sections.body_md:
| Item | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Rod | Medium-light spinning rod, 6-7 ft. |
| Reel | Spinning reel holding ~150 yards of 6-10 lb line. |
| Lures | Classic shad darts and small casting spoons; curly-tail jigs and small crappie jigs also work. |
| Extras | Split shot or a small egg sinker to get light darts/jigs down in faster current. |

sources.label: Outdoor Life, How to Catch Shad, a Beginner's Guide

sections.heading: Technique
sections.body_md:
1. Cast a shad dart or small jig upstream or across the current, let it sink for a second, then start a slow, steady retrieve — keep it moving low, just off bottom, since shad travel low in the water column.
2. Work the lure through the water column with a gentle up-and-down jigging motion, imitating an injured baitfish.
3. Target eddies, the outside of bends, creek mouths, and places where the river widens — shad pause to rest in these calmer pockets before pushing on to the next stretch of current.
4. Since shad aren't feeding, expect strikes to come from putting the lure right in their path repeatedly rather than from a scent or bait appeal — persistence and precise current reads matter more than lure choice.
5. Fish dawn and dusk first if your schedule allows — the light change alone can trigger a short, intense window of activity.

sections.heading: Handling & Release
sections.body_md: Shad have soft mouths and are easy to lose or injure on a hard hookset — use steady rod pressure rather than trout-style hooksets and keep fish in the water as much as possible when unhooking, especially any you intend to release. Given the DFO-flagged concerns around the Saint John River population (see Conservation notes below), practicing careful release on non-retained fish is worth doing even where not strictly mandated.

sections.heading: Conservation & Consumption Notes
sections.body_md:
American shad status varies by watershed and is actively being reviewed. COSEWIC (Canada's species-at-risk assessment body) has listed American shad as a **prioritized candidate species** for a formal status assessment — meaning it is flagged as a species of concern under active review, though it has not (as of the sources reviewed here) received a formal at-risk designation. Separately, the Saint John River's Mactaquac Dam has been a long-standing bottleneck for the population, and DFO has moved to close the Mactaquac Biodiversity Facility that supported it, a signal that this population may be under increasing pressure.

Given both signals, fish this species conservatively: check the current DFO Maritimes/Gulf Region in-season notices for the river you're fishing before your trip, since quotas and any conservation-driven restrictions can change year to year and mid-season, and treat any bag limit or closure notice as taking precedence over general information in this guide.

variants.name: Alewife (Gaspereau)
variants.how_to_tell: Size is the fastest check: American shad run much larger, with adult females reaching up to 30 inches, while alewife top out around 7-9 oz — smaller than any legal-size shad. The jaw is the definitive check on a fish in hand: a shad's lower jaw rises in a gradual slope and tucks into a notch under the upper jaw, while an alewife's (and blueback herring's) lower jaw juts upward sharply in a bent, shovel-like angle.
variants.where_found: Alewife run the same rivers at the same time as American shad throughout NB and NS — the Saint John River and Annapolis system carry both runs concurrently in spring.
variants.notes: Regulatory and conservation status differ: American shad is a COSEWIC prioritized candidate species under active review, while alewife (gaspereau) supports an active commercial fishery in Nova Scotia. Confirm which species you have before assuming either species' rules apply.

variants.name: Blueback Herring (Gaspereau)
variants.how_to_tell: Same size difference as alewife applies here: blueback herring reach only about a pound, far smaller than a legal adult American shad. The jaw check is identical too — a shad's lower jaw slopes gradually into a notch under the upper jaw, while a blueback herring's lower jaw angles up sharply in the same shovel shape as an alewife's.
variants.where_found: Runs the same rivers and same spring window as American shad and alewife across NB and NS, including the Saint John River and Annapolis system.
variants.notes: Same practical concern as alewife: don't assume shad-specific conservation flags or bag rules apply to a smaller river-herring catch, or vice versa — check the jaw and size before deciding what you've caught.
